---
order: 2
unit: causes
title: Why did Qin win?
node: AC9HH7S05 n2
summary: "Explain why a big event happened by finding several causes, not just one. Long-term causes build up over many years; short-term causes come just before; a trigger is the spark that sets the event off at that moment. Then describe the event's effects, both straight away and long afterwards. The worked event is the state of Qin conquering its rivals and unifying China in 221 BCE."
language: maths
hook: "In 230 BCE there were seven rival states in China. Nine years later there was one. Why Qin?"
---
For hundreds of years, China was split into rival states that fought each other. In 221 BCE one of them, **Qin**, had conquered the rest. Its king took a new title: the **First Emperor**.

Historians rarely explain an event like this with one reason. They look for **several causes**, working over different lengths of time:

- **Long-term causes** (also called *underlying* causes) build up over many years. They make the event possible.
- **Short-term causes** happen just before the event.
- A **trigger** is the spark that sets the event off at that moment. It explains *when*, but not on its own *why*.

They also look at **effects**: what the event changed straight away (short-term), and what it changed for a long time afterwards (long-term).

## Predict: why Qin?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students reach for one big reason, the slip this hinge is about."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Why do you think Qin, out of seven rival states, ended up ruling them all?"
  options:
    - "Its farms and army grew strong over a century, then its king used them"
    - "King Zheng was a brilliant leader who outplanned every rival king"
    - "Qin had luck on its side in the last few battles, when it counted"
    - "The other six states were weak, so Qin was bound to beat them"
  actual: "Historians usually point to several causes working together: reforms over a century that made Qin's army and farms strong, grain from irrigated land, and King Zheng's campaigns at the end. No single one explains it alone."
```

## Try: long-term or short-term?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting causes by when they happened turns 'long-term' and 'short-term' into something students can check against dates."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Qin unified China in 221 BCE. Sort each cause: long-term or short-term?"
  options: ["Long-term (many years before)", "Short-term (just before)"]
  items:
    - ["Reforms that gave land and rank to soldiers and farmers, in the 300s BCE", "Long-term (many years before)", "Over a century before 221 BCE."]
    - ["The Dujiangyan waterworks irrigating the Chengdu Plain, from about 256 BCE", "Long-term (many years before)", "About 35 years of extra grain before unification."]
    - ["King Zheng's armies conquering the last six states, 230 to 221 BCE", "Short-term (just before)", "The final campaigns, in the years just before."]
```

Was your guess right? The dates decide which kind each cause is.

## Worked example: putting causes together

Historians usually explain Qin's success something like this. It is one way of putting it together; they still argue about which cause mattered most.

| | Cause | Why it mattered |
|---|---|---|
| Long-term | Reforms in the 300s BCE rewarded farming and fighting with land and rank | Qin had many farmers and soldiers with a reason to work hard |
| Long-term | Dujiangyan (about 256 BCE) watered the Chengdu Plain | More grain to feed big armies far from home |
| Short-term | King Zheng's campaigns, 230 to 221 BCE | Qin used that strength to conquer the six states one after another |

No single row explains the event. Take away the grain and the army can't be fed. Take away the campaigns and Qin is just a strong state, not an empire.

**Effects**

| | Effect |
|---|---|
| Short-term | One ruler over all the former states, with officials sent to run each commandery |
| Long-term | One written script, and standard weights, measures and coins, which later dynasties kept |

Nib's notes below are made up for this lesson.

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Catching Nib's one-cause answer names the hinge slip; the second check separates causes from effects."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "causes.txt#nib"
      text: "Click the first line where Nib's thinking goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: single-cause-event
      explain: "Line 3: Nib turns one cause into the whole explanation. King Zheng's campaigns mattered, but they rested on a century of reforms and the grain to feed his armies."
    hint: ["Could King Zheng have won with no grain and no army?", "Think about what Qin built up long before King Zheng was king. Which of Nib's lines leaves all of that out?"]
    smaller:
      check:
        type: question
        q: "A netball team wins the grand final. Which explanation is best?"
        options:
          - "Hard training all season, a strong defence and a great last quarter"
          - "The captain shot the winning goal, so the win was down to her"
          - "The other team missed a late shot, so really it was luck"
          - "They won the last quarter, and that is the part that decided it"
        answer: 0
        feedback:
          - null
          - "That turns one player into the whole reason. She was one player in a team that had trained all season."
          - "That turns luck into the whole reason. A team does not reach a final by luck alone."
          - "That treats the trigger as the whole reason. The last quarter set off the win; the season's work made it possible."
        explain: "Big results usually have several causes: some build up over time, some happen right at the end."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which of these is an effect of Qin unifying China, not a cause?"
      options:
        - "One written script used across the whole empire"
        - "Reforms rewarding farmers and soldiers in the 300s BCE"
        - "Grain from the irrigated Chengdu Plain"
        - "King Zheng's campaigns against the six states"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "That came long before 221 BCE, so it is a cause, not an effect."
        - "The grain fed Qin's armies before unification: a cause."
        - "The campaigns came before and led to unification: a short-term cause."
      explain: "A cause comes before the event and helps explain it; an effect comes after and is changed by it."
```

### Find Nib's mistake

### Cause or effect?

## Vary: what was the trigger?

In 209 BCE, the year after the First Emperor died, a revolt began. **According to Sima Qian**, a Han court historian writing about a century later, a group of men called up for service were held up by heavy rain. They knew they would arrive late and feared being punished, so they rebelled instead. Revolts spread across the old states, and by 206 BCE the Qin dynasty had fallen.

```step
stage: modify
insight: "The rain story is a clear trigger; separating it from the underlying causes practises the second distinction in the checkpoint."
check:
  type: question
  q: "In Sima Qian's account, which was the trigger for the 209 BCE revolt?"
  options:
    - "Rain held up the men, so they knew they would arrive late"
    - "Years of heavy demands for labour and soldiers across the empire"
    - "People in the conquered states resenting Qin rule"
    - "The First Emperor dying the year before"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "That was building up for years: an underlying cause. Ask what set the revolt off on that day."
    - "That resentment was there long before 209 BCE: an underlying cause, not the spark."
    - "That came before the revolt, but coming before doesn't make it the spark. What set off this group, that day?"
  explain: "The rain was the spark, as Sima Qian tells it. The years of hard demands and resentment explain why one small revolt spread so fast."
```

## Practise: short-term or long-term effects?

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Sorting effects by timescale checks the effects half of the checkpoint on its own."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Sort each effect of Qin unifying China in 221 BCE."
  options: ["Short-term effect", "Long-term effect"]
  items:
    - ["The six rival kings lost their thrones", "Short-term effect", "This happened at once."]
    - ["Officials were sent to run the commanderies", "Short-term effect", "The new empire needed running straight away."]
    - ["Later dynasties kept one written script", "Long-term effect", "It lasted far beyond the Qin."]
    - ["Later dynasties kept the Qin way of running an empire", "Long-term effect", "The Han and dynasties after them kept it."]
```

## Make: causes and effects, in your book

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing their own multi-causal explanation is the checkpoint itself."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I explained one event from the society our class is studying (or Qin unifying China), with at least two causes (one long-term, one short-term) and two effects. A partner read it and gave feedback." }
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

Several causes matter whenever historians ask why something happened. If your class does the course Contact and conflict, you will meet the same idea there, in why societies came into contact and fought.

## Typical: Rome gets an emperor

In 27 BCE, Octavian took the name **Augustus** and became, in practice, Rome's first emperor. For decades before, powerful generals with armies loyal to them had fought each other in civil wars. In 31 BCE Octavian defeated his last rivals, Mark Antony and Cleopatra, at the battle of Actium.

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "The same long-term and short-term split works on Rome, which shows the skill travels."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Sort each cause of Augustus becoming Rome's first emperor in 27 BCE."
  options: ["Long-term", "Short-term"]
  items:
    - ["Decades of civil wars between powerful generals", "Long-term", "A slow build-up over generations."]
    - ["Armies more loyal to their generals than to Rome", "Long-term", "This grew over many years."]
    - ["Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BCE", "Short-term", "Four years before."]
```

## Wider: which cause mattered most?

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Weighing causes is where historians disagree, so this step practises asking what would settle it, not picking a winner."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Two students argue. One says Qin's reforms mattered most; the other says King Zheng's campaigns did. What would help them most?"
  options:
    - "Asking what each cause did, and whether Qin could have won without it"
    - "Choosing whichever cause happened closest to 221 BCE"
    - "Choosing whichever cause the textbook lists first"
    - "Agreeing that every cause mattered exactly the same"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "The latest cause is not always the most important one: that is the trigger slip."
    - "The order a book lists causes in is not an argument."
    - "Historians often argue some causes mattered more. They give reasons."
  explain: "Historians weigh causes by asking what each one did and what would have happened without it, and they back their answer with evidence."
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: explain an event with several causes, sorted into long-term and
  short-term, and describe its short-term and long-term effects
summary: Identify and describe several causes of a historical event, distinguish
  long-term (underlying) from short-term causes and the trigger, and describe
  the event's effects.
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 7 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 5 min · Practise 5
  min · Make 11 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can give at least two causes of a historical event.
  - I can say which causes are long-term, which are short-term and which is the
    trigger.
  - I can describe a short-term and a long-term effect.
struggle: Students settle on one cause, usually a person (the king) or the last
  thing that happened. Keep asking 'and what made that possible?'
before: >-
  AC9HH7S05 n2 (hinge). Kit's hinge reason: students who give single-cause
  accounts cannot later see continuity and change existing together.


  The explanation of Qin's success is labelled in the lesson as "one way of
  putting it together; historians still argue about which cause mattered most"
  (rules T8). The causes used are well supported: Shang Yang's reforms in the
  4th century BCE, which replaced hereditary rank with ranks of merit won mainly
  in war (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Chinese Legalism; Shang Yang died
  in 338 BCE), Dujiangyan (about 256 BCE, UNESCO; also in Shaped by the land),
  and the final campaigns of 230 to 221 BCE. Effects: unified script, measures
  and coins, and commanderies run by officials (The Met), with the
  administrative model kept by later dynasties.


  The 209 BCE revolt is told "according to Sima Qian". He says the penalty for
  lateness was death; Qin legal texts found since suggest lighter penalties, so
  the lesson says only that the men "feared being punished". The last Qin ruler
  surrendered in late 207 BCE; many books date the end to 206 BCE, and the
  lesson says "by 206 BCE". If a student knows the story, this is a good early
  example of why historians check a source (the Historical interpretations
  course comes back to it).


  The contact and conflict lens (AC9HH7K12) also teaches several causes at once
  for wars and contact; mention it if your class has met it, without repeating
  it here.


  Usually Year 7; not yet tried with a class. No board or clips.


  Relevant ACARA AC9HH7S05 elaborations (examples, not a checklist): "sequencing
  events from early Australia and the ancient society in order, using timelines
  to identify and describe causes and effects".


  First Nations: the elaboration names early Australia for sequencing; this
  lesson uses no First Nations example (rules T1). Deep time Australia is taught
  in class with First Nations-led resources.
running:
  - "Predict: list every answer students give on the board, then ask which could
    stand alone."
  - "Try: ask what decides long-term or short-term (the date compared with 221
    BCE)."
  - "Worked example: cover one row of the cause table and ask whether Qin still
    wins."
  - "Vary: ask whether the rain could have started a revolt in a happy, well-fed
    empire."
  - "Make: students write in their own book; a partner checks for one long-term
    and one short-term cause."
stuck:
  - see: A student gives only King Zheng (or only the last battle) as the cause.
    ask: What did he need before he could win? Where did his soldiers and their food
      come from?
    fix: Add the long-term causes that made the campaigns possible.
  - see: A student calls the trigger the main cause.
    ask: Would rain have started a revolt that spread across the empire if people
      were content?
    fix: The trigger explains when; the underlying causes explain why it grew.
  - see: A student lists effects as causes.
    ask: Did this happen before 221 BCE or after?
    fix: Causes come before the event, effects after.
support: Give a two-column card (Before 221 BCE / After 221 BCE) and have
  students place each statement before naming it a cause or an effect.
stretch: Rank the three causes in the table from most to least important and
  give a reason for the top one. What evidence would change your mind?
leads: "Continue to Qin to Han, where several things are happening at once: some
  change, some stay the same."
exit:
  q: Give one long-term cause and one short-term cause of Qin unifying China, and
    one long-term effect.
  a: "For example: reforms in the 300s BCE (long-term); King Zheng's campaigns 230
    to 221 BCE (short-term); one written script kept by later dynasties
    (long-term effect)."
explain: "Big events usually have several causes: long-term causes build up over
  years, short-term causes come just before, and a trigger sets the event off.
  Effects can be short-term or long-term."
sources:
  - title: "Legalism in Chinese Philosophy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy):
      Shang Yang's ranks of merit"
    url: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-legalism/
    checked: 2026-11-01
  - title: Qin Dynasty (221–206 B.C.), The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History
    url: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/qin-dynasty-221-206-b-c
    checked: 2026-11-01
  - title: Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System (UNESCO World
      Heritage List 1001)
    url: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1001
    checked: 2026-11-01
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Think of a time a team, a band or a group you know of did really well. Was
      there only one reason?
    prompts:
      - Which reasons built up over a long time?
      - What happened right at the end?
    notes: Keep examples public (sport, a film, a famous team), not students' own
      lives.
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Take one away
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Show the three causes of Qin's success. Pairs take turns covering one
        and saying whether Qin still wins, and why.
      notes: "Bring out that the causes depend on each other: grain feeds the army the
        reforms built."
  questions:
    - at: make
      title: Check before moving on
      type: question
      q: In Sima Qian's account, rain held up the men who began the 209 BCE revolt.
        What kind of cause was the rain?
      options:
        - The trigger
        - A long-term cause
        - An effect of the revolt
      answer: 0
      explain: It set the revolt off that day; years of hard demands explain why it
        spread.
      feedback:
        - null
        - Rain on one day is not a slow build-up.
        - The rain came before the revolt, so it cannot be its effect.
```
